claims.text: Increasing the concentration of a lattice-distorting element such as Al in an HEA coating improves its wear performance.
The wear improvement from additional Al is caused by enhanced dislocation obstruction.
Increasing the concentration of the lattice-distorting element stabilizes beneficial microstructural phases during wear.
HEA coatings of the proposed type typically exhibit a single-phase or dual-phase microstructure.
Increasing the selected alloying-element concentration enhances lattice distortion.
Enhanced lattice distortion strengthens the HEA microstructure.
Enhanced lattice distortion increases barriers to dislocation motion.
Enhanced lattice distortion stabilizes phases against deformation-induced transformation.
Slower dislocation movement minimizes plastic flow.
Minimizing plastic flow reduces coating wear.
Maintaining a single high-hardness phase helps the coating resist phase degradation under repeated sliding or abrasive contact.
HEA coatings with elevated levels of the selected lattice-distorting element will have greater hardness than the baseline coating.
HEA coatings with elevated levels of the selected lattice-distorting element will have a lower wear rate than the baseline coating.
The proposed beneficial effect should hold under moderate-to-high wear loads and industrially relevant temperatures.
At extreme temperatures, other diffusion-controlled processes may dominate and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Excessive concentrations of the selected element can produce deleterious phases and eliminate the wear benefit.
Prior HEA literature identifies lattice distortion as a contributor to enhanced mechanical and wear-related properties.
Phase instability can degrade the wear performance of the proposed coating.

contradictions.description: The intervention says the selected element will be increased while the overall composition remains balanced, which requires compensating changes in other elemental fractions, whereas the experimental design says all other composition parameters will remain constant.

The boundary excludes concentrations that generate deleterious phases from the mechanism's expected range, but the falsification rule treats formation of such phases as falsifying the hypothesis without requiring that the tested concentration remain inside the stated range.
